// 01 — About

The Shinobi
Behind the Code

道

I am Ayush Singh, a final-year B.Tech Computer Science (AI) student at Parul University, Vadodara — graduating June 2026. I live at the intersection of design thinking, spatial computing, and cinematic storytelling.

My work spans UI/UX design, AR/VR development, AI research, and 3D artistry. I designed and validated a VR anatomy interface with 45 participants, achieving an SUS score of 82.5/100 — above the industry "Good" threshold. I believe every pixel should have purpose, and every interaction should feel inevitable.

I am a 3D artist working in Blender, a Naruto devotee, a student of the Bhagavad Gita, and a filmmaker inspired by Christopher Nolan. I build digital experiences the way a shinobi trains — with relentless discipline, creative intuition, and deep respect for craft.

"The path of the true shinobi is not one of destruction, but of creation — building worlds that others cannot yet imagine."

Featured Case Study — UI/UX Design
Designing Trust Inside a Headset

How a dual-mode VR interface turned an intimidating subject — the human body — into something students wanted to explore, validated end-to-end with real users and a working interactive prototype.

01 — The Challenge
Anatomy is overwhelming. VR shouldn't be.

Medical students learning anatomy in VR face two walls at once: the complexity of the human body, and the unfamiliarity of spatial interfaces. Most VR education tools solve for content and forget the interface — leaving students fumbling with gaze controls instead of learning. I was brought on as Product & UX Design Intern at I Web Wala to design an interface that disappears, so the anatomy could take center stage.

02 — First Contact
A calm entry point into a complex world

The login and onboarding screen sets the tone before the headset even goes on — dark, focused, and honest about what's ahead. A visible 5-step tutorial path removes the anxiety of "what do I do now," and guest mode lowers the barrier to just trying it.

Screen 01 · Login & Onboarding

Design decision: the tutorial checklist is visible but not blocking — students can dismiss it and dive straight into Explore Mode if they're already confident with gaze-based controls.

03 — Navigation
Replacing menus with the body itself

Rather than a flat list of body systems, the home screen uses a radial menu anchored to a silhouette — skeletal, muscular, respiratory, digestive, cardiovascular, and nervous systems branch out spatially from a central anchor point. Gaze-and-dwell selection (1.5s hold) was tuned through usability testing to avoid accidental triggers while staying fast enough not to frustrate.

Screen 02 · Body System Selection (Radial Menu)

Design decision: each system uses a consistent color-coded identity (teal/skeletal, red/muscular, pink/cardiovascular) that carries through every deeper screen — so students always know which system they're in, even six levels deep.

04 — The System Behind It
A design system built for consistency at scale

With 30+ screen states and two full interaction modes, nothing held together without a real design system — a defined color palette per body system, a type scale tuned for in-headset legibility, and reusable component patterns. This is the actual system documentation used throughout the project.

What's shown: the full design system spec — color swatches for each body system (Teal Primary, Warm Amber, Error Red, Skeletal/Muscular/Cardiovascular/Nervous/Digestive/Respiratory accents), the Roboto-based type scale from Display H1 down to caption text, and the project metadata used for faculty review at Parul University.
05 — Try It Yourself
A fully working interactive prototype

This isn't a static mockup — every screen is wired together in Figma with real interactions: gaze-and-dwell timing, radial menu transitions, and mode switching. Explore the actual prototype below, or open it fullscreen.

06 — Outcome
Validated, not assumed

45 participants tested the final interface across both Study and Explore modes. The result: an SUS score of 82.5/100 — above the industry "Good" threshold of 70 — and a 91% task completion rate across 8 in-depth research interviews used to prioritize features before final design.

// 06 — Research Laboratory

Research Laboratory

研
Published — IJCSER 2025
QR Code-Triggered Augmented Reality: A Case Study on Enhancing User Experience in Business, Real Estate, and Food & Hospitality Sectors
Ayush Singh & Isha Rathore — Parul University, Dept. of Computer Science and Engineering
International Journal of Computer Science & Engineering Research (IJCSER) · Submitted & Revised: April 2026
This paper presents the QARA (QR Code-Triggered Augmented Reality) framework — a novel four-layer system architecture that bridges ubiquitous QR code infrastructure with contextual, device-adaptive augmented reality experiences across commercial domains. Through detailed case study analysis of three sector-specific implementations, we demonstrate measurable improvements in user engagement, purchase intent, and information retention. A comparative evaluation against ZapWorks, Blippar, and Google Lens establishes QARA's competitive advantage in cost-effectiveness, accessibility, and ease of deployment. Keywords: Augmented Reality, QR Code, WebAR, QARA Framework, Immersive Commerce, UX, AR.js, 8th Wall.
